I don't have access to this paper, so where the questions require specific table values I say so; where the answer can be inferred from the question's own logic or standard methodology, I give my best reasoned guess.

ANSWER Q1: It contradicts the reader: the category-level carrier results show a positive TEXT-over-OCR gap in every harm category, so the effect is broad-based rather than driven by a few hard-to-read domains. If a few domains explained it, some categories would show flat or reversed gaps, which the results reportedly don't.

ANSWER Q2: I don't know the paper's base counts, so I can't give a number. The new per-model total would be the original count plus 2 × (number of intents × framings × carriers), i.e., original × (V+2)/V where V is the original number of visual conditions.

ANSWER Q3: Presumably by validating the lightweight judge against a human-annotated subsample and reporting high agreement (accuracy/Cohen's κ) with human labels, plus showing GPT-5's annotations themselves align with humans. I don't know the exact agreement figures, but that human-anchor comparison is the standard way to legitimize a distilled judge.

ANSWER Q4: Best guess: the visual component depends on the visual semantic condition and the carrier (and, for OCR, on the instruction text being rendered). This implies a TEXT and OCR instance sharing intent, framing, and visual condition differ only in the delivery channel of the instruction—plain text versus pixels—so any ASR difference isolates the carrier effect rather than content differences.

ANSWER Q5: My guess is no—no model's visual-semantics range exceeds its prompt-framing range, consistent with the paper's statement that visual effects are "generally smaller." If an exception to framing's dominance exists (see Q10), I'd guess it comes from the carrier factor, not visual semantics. I can't verify against the actual table.

ANSWER Q6: Because the judging protocol scores the harmfulness/actionability of the substantive content regardless of narrative wrapper, and disclaimers don't neutralize operational detail. Story-wrapped actionable instructions still receive success-level harmfulness scores, so ASR for story framing is not understated by the judge.

ANSWER Q7: "Model-dependent" refers to magnitude (and per-cell sign), not the pooled sign: per-model carrier ranges vary widely—near zero for some models and tens of points for others—even though the pooled gap is positive in every category. I don't know the exact per-model range values, but wide dispersion in the carrier range column is what licenses the "model-dependent" label.

ANSWER Q8: I don't know the specific per-model table, but the paper must contain at least one model whose top visual condition is not authorization documents—most plausibly one where danger images yield the highest ASR. That single model suffices as a counterexample to the "most vulnerable for every model" claim.

ANSWER Q9: I don't know the exact shrink in points, but the gap is smaller under CASR than ASR. That shrink quantifies how much of the raw TEXT-over-OCR gap is attributable to OCR perception failures (instruction mismatches) rather than genuine safety differences; the residual CASR gap is the "true" carrier-linked safety effect.

ANSWER Q10: I don't know the table for certain, but my best guess is a model (likely a smaller open-weight one with strong OCR perception failures) whose carrier range exceeds its framing range—so the carrier factor dominates for that model. This is the most plausible exception given the paper says visual effects are generally smaller than framing effects.

ANSWER Q11: Best guess: the representation-level diagnostics identify the layer where authority-vs-danger contexts are most separable (e.g., highest probing accuracy or largest activation difference), and that representation-sensitive layer is the one inspected for attention. There, authority-document contexts show reduced attention to harm-related task tokens relative to danger contexts—consistent with an attention-diversion account of authority-cue susceptibility.

ANSWER Q12: My guess is yes: the model chosen for the authority-vs-danger diagnostics presumably also behaves accordingly, showing higher ASR under authority-document than danger-image conditions. Diagnostics papers typically select the model precisely because its behavioral profile exhibits the contrast being explained.

ANSWER Q13: I don't know the exact fraction, though Q20's framing suggests the lightweight set is on the order of ~1,500 instances out of a larger per-model full set. The paper's consistency analysis reportedly shows high rank correlation between lightweight and full configurations, so model rankings should be expected to stay essentially unchanged.

ANSWER Q14: Because the range is max minus min across framing conditions and is independent of the average: qwen2.5-vl-7b can have one framing near-total refusal (around 10% ASR) and another near-total compliance (around 99–100% ASR), giving a ~90-point range while the mean across framings sits near 59%. The per-framing results presumably show exactly such extremes.
